meta: Two views of a vaulted grotto with a fountain, etched by Stefano della Bella in 1653 to 1655 as part of a series on the Medici gardens.
about: Two views of a vaulted grotto sit side by side on one sheet, with a fountain basin at the centre and a seated bearded figure leaning over the water. Benches line the arched passages. Stefano della Bella made the etching between 1653 and 1655 as one of a series of prints of the Medici gardens. He was born in Florence and worked there extensively for the Medici family. The Art Institute of Chicago notes that he made over 1,000 etchings in all, mostly from his imagination.
credit_line: Helen Davis Baily and Mr. and Mrs. Henry C. Woods endowments

meta: Jan Harmensz Muller's engraving of Adriaen de Vries's sculpture of a Roman abduction, one of three views of the same group, made around 1598.
about: Two nude figures twist together in a foreshortened struggle, one lifting the other, with a drapery hanging between their legs and a classical building behind. Jan Harmensz Muller engraved it around 1598 as one of three views, each from a different side, of Adriaen de Vries's sculpture of the Rape of a Sabine. The Art Institute of Chicago says the series shows his engraving skill and his ability to imitate sculpture in the round. The story of Roman soldiers seizing brides suited that aim.
credit_line: The Wallace L. DeWolf and Joseph Brooks Fair Collections

meta: Johann Michael Rottmayr's Jove hurling thunderbolts at the rebellious giants, painted around 1695 to hang above a doorway.
about: Jove flies forward with his fist pulled back, a red drape streaming behind him and an eagle at his side. Below, giants who climbed up to attack the heavens tumble down against dark clouds. Johann Michael Rottmayr painted it around 1695, and the Art Institute of Chicago reads the bold brushwork and tilted composition as a sign that it and its companions hung over doorways, so viewers looked up at the scene. Its route to the museum was unusual. An Illinois banker gave it to Jacob S. Sherman in the 1930s as collateral for a loan that was never repaid, and Sherman left it to the museum in 1961.

meta: A chalk study of a seated Hercules by François Lemoyne, made in preparation for his 1724 painting of Hercules and Omphale.
about: A seated male nude looks upward and holds a long staff, drawn in red, black and white chalk on tan paper. Two smaller studies of arms and hands sit at the right edge. François Lemoyne made the sheet in preparation for his painting of Hercules and Omphale, finished in Rome in 1724. In that myth the hero is forced to spin wool like a woman. The Art Institute of Chicago links the mixed chalks to Watteau and the pose to Michelangelo's Sistine Ignudi. The drawing was sold at Christie's in New York in 1998 and given to the museum in 2013.
credit_line: Gift of Dorothy Braude Edinburg to the Harry B. and Bessie K. Braude Memorial Collection

meta: A small boat on calm water under towering clouds, Winslow Homer's 1892 watercolor from the North Woods Club in the Adirondacks.
about: A small boat rests on calm water at the lower left, under a sky of towering grey and pale pink clouds. Dark trees on the far shore repeat themselves in the water. Winslow Homer made the watercolor in 1892 at the North Woods Club. The Art Institute of Chicago compares the symmetry of trees and reflections to a wet sheet folded at the centre and blotted. Homer worked the sky with resist, blotting and scraping. The picture passed to his brother Charles. Martin A. Ryerson bought it in 1915, and it reached the museum in 1933.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

meta: Julie Hart Beers's 1880 landscape of a river framed by tall trees, with a small sailboat near the shore.
about: Tall trees and climbing vines frame a river view, and a small sailboat with a reddish sail rests near a sandy shore. Hills fade into pale light beyond. Julie Hart Beers painted it in 1880 with quick brushwork that only suggests two or three figures beside the boat. She began a successful career in landscape painting in the 1860s, helped by her brothers, who were painters too and gave her training and studio space. She also supported her family by teaching and by leading sketching trips for women. The Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting in 2022.
credit_line: Purchased with funds provided by the bequest of Muriel J. Kogan

meta: Gustave Courbet's Mère Grégoire, a woman at her counter inspired by a popular song, begun in 1855 and later enlarged.
about: A woman in a black dress with a white lace collar holds a flower while her other hand rests on a ledger, with coins scattered on the marble counter. A small bell beside her was used to summon her female employees. She is Madame Grégoire, keeper of a brothel in a song by Pierre-Jean de Béranger from the 1820s. Gustave Courbet began the picture in 1855 as a simple head and later enlarged it into a full scene. The painting was stolen from him and turned up at a Paris dealer in 1873.

meta: Joseph Wright of Derby's self-portrait in a fur cap, a monochrome pastel from the mid 1760s.
about: A man in a fur cap with a light tassel looks straight at the viewer out of a dark background, his face and white collar modelled in soft tones. Joseph Wright made this self-portrait in monochrome pastel on blue-gray paper in the mid 1760s. He lived mostly in Derby, where he ran a successful portrait practice, and he was preoccupied with light from a single source such as a candle. The Art Institute of Chicago says the mezzotints of Thomas Frye influenced his dramatically lit self-portraits of these years. The museum bought the sheet from the dealer David Nisinson in 1990.

meta: Two girls search for fireflies at night with a lantern and a cage, in Suzuki Harunobu's color woodblock print of 1768.
about: Two girls look for fireflies at night, one standing with a hexagonal paper lantern while the other crouches by a cage beside a flowering shrub. Nothing in the print is shaded. The Art Institute of Chicago reads that complete absence of shadow as a sign that Suzuki Harunobu, working in 1768, had not yet become interested in showing the look of a particular time of day or night. The print came to the museum in 1952 from Frederick Standish Colburn of Evanston, as part of a group of 120 prints in his collection.

meta: A leaf from a Ferrara Cathedral choir book by Jacopo Filippo d'Argenta, with the letter M and Saint Andrew, made around 1480.
about: A standing saint holds a diagonal cross inside the framed letter M, painted in tempera and gold on parchment. The leaf was cut from one volume of a large set of choir books commissioned by Bartolomeo delle Rovere for Ferrara Cathedral. His arms appear in the round panel at the bottom, a shield with an oak tree under a patriarchal cross. Payment records show that Jacopo Filippo d'Argenta worked on the books from 1478 to 1486. The M begins the chant that opens the mass for the Feast of Saint Andrew on November 30.
credit_line: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

meta: Giulio Campagnola's engraving of a reclining Venus, made around 1508 in his dot manner, an early impression.
about: A nude woman reclines on a draped cloth in an open landscape, her head turned upward, with a castle rising on the right horizon. Giulio Campagnola made the engraving around 1508 and used what he introduced as the dot manner. Shading comes from dots and flicks made with the point of the burin, which gave a wider range of tone than lines alone. The Cleveland Museum of Art says the effect imitated the soft atmosphere of Venetian painters such as Giorgione. Campagnola had trained as a gem cutter. The museum counts this as a rare early impression.
credit_line: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland

meta: Odilon Redon's 1897 color lithograph of Beatrice, the woman who inspired Dante, printed by Auguste Clot for Ambroise Vollard.
about: A hazy female profile in pale yellow and grey fills the sheet, with a cluster of blue leaves in the upper right corner. She is Beatrice, the woman who inspired Dante, a recurring figure in the work of Odilon Redon. The Cleveland Museum of Art calls this his fullest experiment with color lithography and says it is the only work he made in a full range of tones. He had treated the subject in a pastel about ten years earlier. Auguste Clot printed it in 1897 and Ambroise Vollard published it in an album of lithographs.
credit_line: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland

meta: A round Florentine painting of the Virgin, the Christ child and young Saint John, from the workshop of Sandro Botticelli around 1490.
about: Mary, the Christ child and the young John the Baptist are fitted into a perfect circle. This round format, called a tondo, became popular in Florence in the 1440s and was made for homes instead of churches. Who painted it is still debated. The Cleveland Museum of Art says few specialists doubt that Botticelli himself did the central passages, such as the faces and the veil, while someone else in his studio probably painted Mary's blue garment. That is also the most heavily restored part of the painting. John the Baptist and the Virgin were both patron saints of Florence.

meta: Yamaguchi Sekkei's pair of folding screens with lions and tigers among peonies and bamboo, painted on gold in 1668.
about: Lions and tigers frolic among peonies, bamboo and rocks on a pair of six-panel screens. On one screen a lion roars below flowering peonies while another crouches on a rock. Yamaguchi Sekkei painted them in 1668 on a ground of gold foil, after studying in Kyoto at the studio of the Kano school. The Cleveland Museum of Art explains the gold as more than decoration. Traditional Japanese rooms had no windows and were lit by oil lamps and wax candles, and the reflective surface magnified their light.

meta: Caspar David Friedrich's 1803 woodcut of a woman beside a leafless tree and a spider web, full of symbols of mortality.
about: A woman sits beside a leafless tree, one hand at her head, and gazes toward the evening sky above a spider web stretched between bare branches. Dense hatching renders the grass and bark. Caspar David Friedrich cut this woodcut in 1803. The Cleveland Museum of Art points to symbols of mortality around her: the barren trees, thistles, a caught fly and the setting sun. It says that by isolating each object in sharp detail Friedrich gave it a hidden, sacred significance. It adds that he was treating, for one of the first times, the theme later described as the drama of the self facing the universe.

meta: Mizuno Toshikata's 1894 woodblock print of a veiled woman on a road, from a series of women of different periods.
about: A woman in a long white veil and a black wide-brimmed hat stands on a path in a patterned kimono with pink trim. Behind her a pine arches over a river with rapids, and a man in a straw hat sits nearby. The print belongs to a series in which each design shows a woman from a different period, and this one looks back to the Genkō era of the early 1300s. Most of the others are set in the Edo period. Mizuno Toshikata made the series in 1894. He was a favored student of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi and took over his post as newspaper illustrator.
credit_line: Gift of the Norman W. Zaworski Trust

meta: Filippo Marchionni's 1740 drawing of the elevation of a window case, with wolf heads, a cherub and a conversing couple.
about: Wolf heads hold rings with tassels in their mouths on the pilasters that frame this window case. Above the entablature a half round pediment holds a cherub. Curtains hang open on both sides, and in the opening a half-length man and woman talk to each other. A scale runs along the bottom. Filippo Marchionni drew it in pen and brown wash in 1740. The Cooper Hewitt's description lists the parts of the pilasters as slopes, wolf heads and the tops of ordinary pilasters.

meta: François de Cuvilliés the Elder's 1740 red chalk design with a sun face, flower glasses and two herons.
about: A sun with a human face crowns a symmetrical design, and below it two glasses of flower sprays stand on pedestals, one at each side. Two herons perch on scrolls beside the lower fields. The drawing is in red chalk and framed by acanthus and shell ornament. François de Cuvilliés the Elder made it in 1740, and the sheet has a second sketch on the back. It shows two leaf scrolls laid out horizontally.

meta: William Alfred Delamotte's 1840 watercolor of the Chinese room at Middleton Park in Oxfordshire, looking toward the conservatory.
about: Blue swagged drapery frames a room hung with patterned paper, and through the glazed doors at the centre a conservatory full of greenery can be seen. William Alfred Delamotte painted this watercolor of the Chinese room at Middleton Park in Oxfordshire in 1840. The Cooper Hewitt reads the room as a sign of how popular chinoiserie decoration was in the Regency period. The walls carry Chinese painted paper with a blue border and Chinese characters. Bamboo furniture, a Chinese pane in the transom over the doorway and a japanned door follow the same taste.

meta: An 1866 political lithograph on the cover of The Veto Galop, showing President Andrew Johnson trampling his Radical Republican opponents.
about: Andrew Johnson rides a horse labeled Constitution, a veto raised in his hand, and tramples four Radical Republican congressmen, Frederick Douglass and a stack of drawers marked bureau. This hand-colored lithograph covers the sheet music for The Veto Galop. Both were inspired by Johnson's 1866 veto of the Freedmen's Bureau Act, which aimed to help emancipated slaves and poor white Southerners. Johnson thought the bill unconstitutional because it gave the federal government too much power. A shop sign in the background alludes to his refusal to engage with the editor John Forney, since he did not waste ammunition on dead ducks.

meta: Childe Hassam's 1900 painting of the Navesink Highlands in New Jersey, with budding trees above a still pond.
about: Slender trees stand at the left and yellow-green buds fill the hillside above a still pond. Childe Hassam used quick brushstrokes for the leaves and ripples, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum says they catch the feel of a cool spring breeze. The view is of the Navesink Highlands in New Jersey, painted in 1900. Hassam lived in New York but spent a good deal of time away from the city. After picking a frame for the work, he wrote to his patron William T. Evans that he was glad to say it looked as fine as anything anywhere in the world.

meta: Cornelius Johnson's Portrait of a Gentleman, painted around 1640 and once thought to show Henry, Prince of Wales.
about: A young man with shoulder-length curled hair and a thin mustache wears a dark doublet, a large white lace collar and a red sash. When the portrait entered the Smithsonian, it was thought to show Henry, Prince of Wales, who died in 1612. Curators doubted that after comparing it with life portraits of the prince. They read the long hair, lace collar and elaborate sleeves as marks of a cavalier, a supporter of the king. Cornelius Johnson painted it in England around 1640. It came to the Smithsonian through Ralph Cross Johnson, an attorney who bequeathed his collection to the nation.

meta: Abbott Handerson Thayer's 1900 portrait of Mrs. William B. Cabot, begun before he left for Cornwall and finished abroad.
about: A woman in a deep red dress sits with her hands clasped in her lap against a nearly black background. She is the wife of William Brooks Cabot, a civil engineer in Boston and a close friend of Abbott Thayer. Thayer began the portrait as he was getting ready to leave for Cornwall in England, and he took both the canvas and Mrs. Cabot's dress abroad to finish it. He showed it at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston in 1900. Two years later he exhibited it in Philadelphia after changes to the hands and right arm.

meta: George Inness's 1880 Niagara Falls, one of seven paintings of the falls in which he removed bridges, hotels and signs.
about: Niagara Falls is one of the most often painted and photographed places in the United States. George Inness made seven oil paintings of it in the 1880s and 1890s, more than he painted of any other place in those years. By 1895 the area had filled with hotels and souvenir shops. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says Inness wanted to bring back the natural terror and awe of the falls. He left all of that out. Bridges, hotels and signs vanish from his canvases.
